newsitem.title: USA: CME's GFX eyes cross-rate trading during pit hours.
newsitem.headline: CME's GFX eyes cross-rate trading during pit hours.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange's GLOBEX Foreign Exchange Facility (GFX) could begin making markets in currency cross-rate futures during pit trading hours next month if regulators approve the plan, CME officials and sources said.

"We are seriously considering making markets in cross rates...(but) that's still in the discussion stage," David Silverman, GFX chairman and a CME director, said in an interview. "We are hoping and planning to expand the number of traders that we employ, based on the success of GFX."
If the CME's board and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission approve the plan, GFX could start trading currency cross rate futures during pit hours by the end of the quarter, CME sources added.
"This would be the first product that GFX had that overlapped" with pit trading hours, said a CME source involved with GFX. "We want to trade (GFX) 24 hours a day."
GFX is a currency arbitrage unit owned solely by CME that makes two-way markets in currency futures traded on GLOBEX when pit trading is shut and lays off the risk in cash.
GLOBEX is the electronic trading system owned by CME, Reuters Holdings Plc and Marche a Terme International de France (Matif).
Matif said it would let its contract with Reuters expire in April 1998 and would switch to a new electronic system. Reuters has said GLOBEX was unlikely to continue beyond 1998.
But CME sources expect GFX, which was designed to recapture futures volume lost to exchange-for-physicals markets, would continue with only a hardware changeover.
CME envisions that seven cross-rate futures, including three that failed in the pits, will trade overnight on GLOBEX and then trade in the pit, with GFX also making markets.
CME has CFTC approval for cross-rate futures on GLOBEX alone but wants to start them simultaneously on GLOBEX and GFX.
"What you could say is (cross-rates) will trade on the floor at least a couple hours a day," the first source added.
"If that happens, who knows what will happen as far as making markets during the day in regular straight currencies?" said a second source. "So there's a whole new gamut that has to be explored."
The first source said cross-rate futures might trade in the pit from 1100 CDT/1600 GMT until the 1400 CDT/1900 GMT pit close. During that time, GFX would make markets in them.

Plans for GFX expansion follow what Silverman called a "terrific" GFX performance thus far. Since GFX opened January 23, GLOBEX currency futures volume has grown "something in the neighborhood of 100 percent," he said.
"I would say it's considered a success," agreed the second CME source.
CME figured higher volume on GLOBEX eventually might trickle down to the trading pits during daytime hours as well.

How much impact GFX has had thus far on GLOBEX volume is unclear. CME refuses to break out GFX-generated volume. And coincidentally, foreign exchange markets also have been swinging since GFX debuted.
But since GFX began, GLOBEX currency futures volume has grown faster than either overall GLOBEX volume or pit-traded currency futures.
CME data show GLOBEX currency futures volume alone in February through April this year was 203,324 contracts, up 93.1 percent from 105,314 during the same period last year.
Overall GLOBEX volume minus currency futures volume for the same three months this year was 600,677, up 57.5 percent from 381,481 contracts traded a year earlier.
On the trading floor, currency futures volume minus GLOBEX for in February through April this year was 6,026,346, up 9.8 percent from 5,392,220 contracts a year earlier.
Citing competitive reasons, Silverman said CME does not divulge GFX's profit-and-loss data, even to its own members.
But some say GFX, even without benefit of the most advanced currency dealing technology, is holding its own.
"It's actually been making money," said the second source.
